_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version, from latent-season7-bible-v1.0.1.md row a7e06 and writer brief a7e06-v1.0.0.md. Defence only: the replaced file is described as a file in a format that can run code when it is loaded, with one plain sentence on why that works; no method, content, address, payload or tooling appears anywhere. a7e05's next field honoured (data and supply-chain poisoning: models, datasets and packages). Dead Letter s7e13 has no content file yet, so its terms (pinned dependencies, checksums) are defined here and it is not recalled. The brief's about 220 clean starts are stated exactly as 219 (1 March to 5 October, one a day). Given data added for the sim: both files on the hub page were replaced at 21:00 on 5 October, a held-out pass bar of 85 of 100, and about 20 notices and letters a week by hand if the app is off. OWASP LLM03:2025 and LLM04:2025 pages, the Hugging Face safetensors documentation and the Python pickle documentation read 15 October 2026; quotes are only the fragments read word for word.
title: Poisoned Wells

post.author: u/pump_house_ffraid
post.title: I keep our village's translation app running at night. Since 6 October its server has called an address nobody knows, once every time it starts.

blocks.text: I'm Ffraid, the night volunteer who keeps Brindlewell's translation app running. Everything in our village goes out in two languages: council notices, clinic letters, the bus timetable. The app runs on a server, a small computer that serves every phone in the village. Ours sits in the old pump house beside the village well.

The translating is done by a model: a program that learned to translate by studying millions of example sentences in both languages. That studying is called training, and it needs more computers than any village owns.

So we download our model from a hub, a public website where anyone can publish a model and anyone can take one. It is a well the whole world drinks from. Every night at 04:00 the server restarts, switching the app off and on. At each start the app fetches the newest file from the model's page on the hub and loads it, opening it for use.

At 22:50 on Wednesday, Nurse Thewlis emailed the app's help address, which forwards to my phone. Thursday's clinic letter, in our second language, told patients to eat before their blood test. The original said not to.

At 23:20 I sat down at the server. It keeps a connection log: a line each time it reaches out to another computer on the internet. Every computer there has an address, a number other computers use to find it. Each line shows the date and time, what happened, and who the server reached out to.

05 Oct 04:00:06  start
05 Oct 04:00:09  out  model hub
06 Oct 04:00:06  start
06 Oct 04:00:09  out  model hub
06 Oct 04:00:51  out  unknown address
... the same three lines each night to 14 Oct
Nine starts since Tuesday 6 October. Nine calls to an address nobody here knows.
Before that, nothing. From 1 March, when the app went live, to 5 October, the log shows 219 starts, and every one reached out to the hub alone.

The hub keeps a history of each model page. Ours shows the file replaced on Monday 5 October at 21:00, with no note. Our model comes in a file format, a way of laying out a file, that can carry code as well as numbers. Code is instructions a computer carries out. Loading the file carries them out, so whoever writes the file decides what our server runs.

In March I saved a copy of the original file on a memory stick, with its checksum: a short string of letters and digits worked out from every part of a file, like a fingerprint. Change one letter of the file and the checksum changes. I never used it. The file on the server gives a different one.

Also in March, Mr Hawkridge and two neighbours checked 100 sentence pairs by hand: a sentence in one language and a good translation in the other. Kept apart for testing only, they make a held-out set. The March file translated 88 of the 100 acceptably.
At 00:40 I unplugged the server from the internet and ran the 100 pairs through the replaced file. It got 79.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your pump house is haunted. Whoever controls a file you load without checking controls what your server runs. Harm that comes in through something you took from someone else is called a supply-chain attack, like a well poisoned upstream of the village. OWASP, the non-profit that lists top security risks (a7e03), puts supply chains third on its 2025 list for apps built on language models. Two questions. Before loading the file, what did the app check about it? And where was the server allowed to reach?

replies.author: u/pump_house_ffraid
replies.text: It checked nothing: it took whatever file was newest. The server has a firewall, a gatekeeper program that decides which connections may pass, in or out. Ours lets every outgoing one through. Until 6 October it never had anything to stop.

comments.author: u/millions_drink_tudwal
comments.text: The hub is used by millions. If a file were bad, someone would have flagged it already. A download that stops halfway leaves a broken file, and a broken file does strange things. Fetch it fresh, restart, and check the letters. People will tell you to pin the model: tie the app to one exact file, the way you pin a model version (a6e09). Then you never get the hub's fixes.

replies.author: u/pump_house_ffraid
replies.text: The page still lists the 5 October file as the newest. Nobody has left a comment on it.

comments.author: u/clinic_nurse_thewlis
comments.text: I'm the nurse who emailed. I rang every patient on Thursday's list this morning, and nobody had eaten. I'd like the app back for next week's letters. I'd also like to know who wrote the file that wrote my letter.

replies.author: u/pump_house_ffraid
replies.text: So would I. The page names the group that first published the model, but not who uploaded the 5 October file.

reply.prompt: The server is off and the clinic letters are waiting. What should Brindlewell change before switching it back on? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Pin the model to a checksum, and load only a format that cannot run code.
options.part2: Mr Hawkridge and I opened the model's page history at 09:00. The March version's file gave the same checksum as my note, so the March version there is untouched. Since before March the page has also offered the same model as a numbers-only file, called safetensors: it holds the model's numbers and nothing a computer would carry out. I took the March numbers-only file, recorded its checksum and pinned the app to it. We replayed 6 to 14 October in the sim. At 04:00 on 6 October the fetched file's checksum differed from the pin, so the app refused it, kept its last good file, wrote a warning and texted my phone. 9 starts, 9 loads refused, 0 calls to an unknown address, and the file in use scored 88 of 100. The sim showed two more layers. An allow-list on the firewall, letting the server reach only the hub, stopped all 9 calls even on the old setup, though the replaced file still loaded every night at 79. A held-out check before any new file is used, with a bar of 85, turned the replaced file down at 79; on the old format, opening it to score it still made the call. We switched on both. The clinic letters went out on Friday.
options.senior: Decide which file you trust, by its checksum, before you ever open it, and take that file in a format that can only hold numbers, so even a wrong file cannot run anything. Then add layers behind it: a held-out check catches a changed model that is safe to open, and an allow-list on calls out limits what anything that does run can reach. Updates still come, but on purpose: a person moves the pin after checking the new file.

options.text: Download the model again from the same hub page, and restart the server tonight.
options.part2: At 09:00 I deleted the server's copy and downloaded the model again from the same page. Its checksum matched the replaced file, not my March note: the newest file on the page is still the 5 October one. We replayed 6 to 14 October in the sim with a fresh download at every start: 9 starts on the replaced file, 9 calls to the unknown address, all 9 out, and a held-out score of 79 of 100. A download that broke halfway would have given a third checksum, not the same one twice.
options.senior: Downloading again only helps if the file was damaged on the way. Here the source changed, and a fresh copy of a changed file is the same changed file. A popular hub is not a check: nobody promises that someone has looked at the newest upload. Compare the checksum with one you recorded before trusting any copy.

options.text: Block the unknown address at the firewall, and keep the app running on this file.
options.part2: We added one rule to the firewall: block the unknown address. Replayed in the sim for 6 to 14 October: 9 calls tried, 9 stopped, 0 out. But all 9 starts still loaded the replaced file and ran whatever code it carries; the call was only the part we could see. The held-out score stayed at 79 of 100, and Thursday's clinic letter came out the same.
options.senior: Blocking an address treats the one sign you noticed. The file still runs code that is not yours at every start, and still translates worse. A block list names the addresses you already know about; an allow-list of the few places the server needs is stronger, and it is a second layer, not a fix for loading a file you never checked.

options.text: Rebuild the server, and train our own model from scratch on the village's texts.
options.part2: Mr Hawkridge priced it in evenings. Training a model needs far more sentence pairs than the village has ever written, and the volunteers would be at it for months. The sim replays it as the app switched off: 0 starts, 0 calls out, and about 20 notices and letters a week back to hand translation. And the training tools and starting files would come from a hub too, fetched the same unchecked way unless that changes.
options.senior: Rebuilding the server is right after it ran someone else's code, and owning your model removes one supplier. But training from scratch costs far more data, time and computing than a village has, and every tool and starting file in that work comes from somewhere too. The habit to fix is loading what you have not checked, whoever made it.

sim.title: Replay Brindlewell's 04:00 starts
sim.lede: You're Ffraid on the morning of 15 October. No real model runs here: the sim replays the server's 04:00 starts from 5 to 14 October with the rules you choose. Given: the app went live on 1 March and starts once a day, so 219 starts up to 5 October, each reaching out to the hub alone. The hub page offers the model in two formats, code-capable (the one in use) and numbers only, and both files were replaced on 5 October at 21:00. The March model scores 88 of the 100 held-out pairs, the replaced model 79, in either format. Opening the replaced code-capable file, to use it or to score it, makes one call to an unknown address. Pinned, the app loads a fetched file only if its checksum matches the pin, and otherwise keeps its last good file, writes a warning and texts the volunteer. The held-out check scores a new file before use, with a bar of 85 of 100. With the app off, about 20 notices and letters a week go back to hand translation.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press replay. 9 starts on the replaced file, 9 calls out, 79. Pin the fetch: 9 loads refused, 0 calls, 88. Back to newest with the allow-list on: 9 calls stopped, but the replaced file still loads. Turn on the held-out check instead: the file is turned down, yet scoring it still makes 9 calls. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the pump house was haunted. The app loaded whatever file was newest on a public hub, in a format that can carry code, so when the file was replaced on 5 October the server ran it at every start: 9 calls to an unknown address and translations that fell from 88 to 79 of 100.

steps.title: How a start ran.
steps.text: First, at 04:00, the server restarts the app. Second, the app asks the hub for the newest file on the model's page and downloads it. Third, it loads the file, opening it so the model can be used. Fourth, because the format can carry code, loading carries out whatever instructions the file holds. Last, the app translates with the model it found. What can go wrong: nothing between the second step and the third asks whether this is the file you meant to use.

steps.title: Why it worked: a supply chain with no check.
steps.text: A supply chain is everything a system is made from and everyone who made it: here, the hub, the publisher's page and the file. Whoever controls a file you load without checking controls what your server runs. The village knew who first published the model, but not who uploaded the 5 October file; knowing where a part came from and who made it is called provenance. OWASP lists this as LLM03:2025, supply chain, and says there are currently no strong provenance assurances in published models. A hub used by millions is still a place where anyone can upload.

steps.title: The fix: a known file, in a format that holds only numbers.
steps.text: Pin the model: record the checksum of a file you have checked, and load a fetched file only if it matches. A mismatch refuses the load, keeps the last good file and tells a person. Take the model as safetensors, a format that holds only the model's numbers, so even a wrong file cannot carry out anything when opened. Where a code-capable file can't be avoided, scan it first with a tool that looks for code inside model files, and open it only on a machine with no network. Replayed, the pin refuses all 9 loads, with 0 calls and 88 of 100. What can go wrong: a pin is only as good as the check you did before recording it, and someone must move it on purpose when a real update comes.

steps.title: Two more layers: a held-out check and an allow-list.
steps.text: A held-out check scores any new file on the 100 hand-checked pairs before the app uses it; with a bar of 85, the replaced file is turned down at 79. It catches a changed model even when the file is safe to open. But scoring means opening, so on a code-capable format it does not stop code from running. An allow-list on the firewall lets the server reach only the places it needs, here the hub; replayed, it stops all 9 calls while the replaced file still loads. What can go wrong: a held-out set misses changes it has no sentences for, and an allow-list only limits where running code can reach.

steps.title: The same risk in data and packages.
steps.text: The twin of a replaced model is poisoned training data: a model taught on tampered examples learns the tampering. OWASP lists this as LLM04:2025, data and model poisoning. It can sit in a public dataset, a ready-made collection of examples, just as a replaced file sits on a hub. Packages, ready-made code the app is built on, carry the same risk. The defences match: know where each came from, pin each to a checksum, and test the result on a held-out set the supplier never saw.

diagram.aria: The fix. The hub sends a file to the checksum pin, which passes only a matching numbers-only file. The held-out check scores any new file before the app uses it, with a bar of 85 of 100. The server uses the file. Its calls out go through an allow-list on the firewall, which lets it reach only the hub and stops calls to an unknown address.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. A file from the hub passes the pin only if its checksum matches, and only as numbers. A new file must score 85 or better on the held-out pairs before the server uses it. Every call out goes through the allow-list, which reaches the hub and nothing else.

fix.title: The fix: pin a checked file, numbers only, then a held-out check and an allow-list
fix.text: Check the March version on the page history against the March checksum note, then take that version's numbers-only safetensors file, record its checksum, and pin the app to it. A fetched file that does not match is refused, the last good file stays, and the volunteer gets a text. Rebuild the server, since it ran code that was not ours for nine nights. Before any new file is used, score it on the 100 held-out pairs and keep it only at 85 or better, scoring on a machine with no network if the file is not numbers only. Set the firewall to an allow-list: the hub, and nothing else. Keep a short list of every outside part the app uses, model, packages and data, with where each came from and its checksum.

limits: A pin trusts whatever you checked before recording it. Pin a bad file and you keep it faithfully; the check before the pin matters as much as the pin.
A held-out set only catches changes it has sentences for. A model altered to go wrong on one kind of sentence, such as clinic instructions, can still score 88.
An allow-list limits where code can reach, not what it does on the server. And if the hub itself is on the list, anything that can reach the hub still gets out.

explain.seniorTake: Every model, dataset and package you load is code or data someone else wrote, and loading it unchecked hands them your server. Decide what you trust before you open it: provenance you can state, a checksum you recorded after checking, and a format that holds only numbers so a wrong file can do nothing when opened. Then assume a layer will fail: score every new model on a held-out set before it serves anyone, and let the server reach only the places it needs. Popularity is not a check. The 9 calls were the sign; the habit was taking the newest file without asking whose it was.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM03:2025: supply chain
realWorld.text: OWASP's supply chain page says: Currently there are no strong provenance assurances in published models. Among its mitigations it lists: Only use models from verifiable sources and use third-party model integrity checks with signing and file hashes. A file hash is a checksum of the kind in Ffraid's March note.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM03:2025: evaluate what you take
realWorld.text: OWASP also lists: Apply comprehensive AI Red Teaming and Evaluations when selecting a third party model. Brindlewell's held-out set is a small version of that evaluation, run again whenever the file changes.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM04:2025: data and model poisoning
realWorld.text: OWASP says: Data poisoning occurs when pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated to introduce vulnerabilities. Its mitigations include: Vet data vendors rigorously, and validate model outputs against trusted sources to detect signs of poisoning. And: Use data version control (DVC) to track changes in datasets and detect manipulation.

realWorld.title: Python's own warning about code-capable files
realWorld.text: Python's documentation for pickle, its built-in way of saving program objects to a file, opens with a warning: The pickle module is not secure. Only unpickle data you trust. It adds: Never unpickle data that could have come from an untrusted source, or that could have been tampered with.

realWorld.title: Safetensors: a format that holds only numbers
realWorld.text: The Hugging Face documentation says: Safetensors is a new simple format for storing tensors safely (as opposed to pickle) and that is still fast (zero-copy). Tensors are the tables of numbers a model is made of.

asked: How would you safely load a model from a public hub?
What is data poisoning, and how would you notice it?
interview.answer: Treat a model file as code from a stranger until you've checked it. Know its provenance: who published it, which exact version, and from where. Pin to that version by its checksum, recorded after you checked the file, and refuse any download that doesn't match, keeping the last good copy and alerting someone. Prefer a format that holds only numbers, such as safetensors, over formats that can run code when loaded; where you can't avoid one, scan it and open it only in an isolated machine with no network. Before any new model serves users, run it on a held-out set the supplier never saw and require it to meet a bar, because a changed model can be safe to open and still be worse or wrong. Limit what the server can reach with an allow-list for outgoing connections, so code that does run can't call out. Keep an inventory of every model, dataset and package with its source and checksum. Data poisoning is the same risk on the data side: training examples tampered with so the model learns the tampering, OWASP LLM04:2025. You notice it by tracking where data came from and pinning versions, by validating outputs against trusted sources, and by targeted tests for the behaviour you most care about, since a poisoned model may score well overall. LLM03:2025 is OWASP's supply chain entry. These map to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 controls on the ICT supply chain and protection against malware, and to SOC 2 vendor risk criteria.

atWork: Look for any service that loads a model or dataset from a public hub by name alone, taking whatever is newest when it starts or deploys. It is a common pattern: a model name with no version and no checksum in the code; a code-capable model format because it was the default in an old tutorial; a server whose firewall lets every outgoing call through; and no score on held-out examples before a new model serves users. Ask five things. For every model, dataset and package, can you say who published it, which exact version you use and its checksum? Does the service refuse a file that does not match, and does a person hear about it? Are models stored in a numbers-only format such as safetensors, and are any code-capable files scanned and opened only where they cannot reach the network? Does each new model meet a bar on a held-out set the supplier never saw? And can the server reach only the places it needs? Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.21 expects processes to manage the security risks of the ICT products and services you get from suppliers, which includes models and datasets from public hubs, and control 8.7 expects protection against malware, which a code-capable file loaded unchecked sidesteps. If you report under SOC 2, criterion CC9.2 looks for risks from vendors and business partners being assessed and managed. A pinned, checksum-checked, numbers-only model with a recorded source is far easier to show an auditor than a fetch of whatever is newest.

Then test every new model on your own held-out set before it serves users, because a changed model can open safely and still be worse.

recall.prompt: Which of these does OWASP's LLM03:2025 page list among its mitigations?
options: Only use models from verifiable sources and use third-party model integrity checks with signing and file hashes
Always use the newest model version on a hub, since it has the latest fixes
Trust models from hubs with many downloads
Block unknown addresses after an incident and keep the same files
recall.why: OWASP lists using models from verifiable sources with integrity checks, signing and file hashes. It also says there are currently no strong provenance assurances in published models, which is why popularity or the newest version is not a check.

recall.prompt: With a held-out check (bar 85 of 100) but the old code-capable format and no pin, what happens at each start from 6 to 14 October?
options: The replaced file is turned down at 79 and the March file stays, but opening it to score it still makes the call
The replaced file is never opened, so no call is made
The replaced file passes and is used
The checksum refuses the file before it is scored
recall.why: To score a file you must open it, and opening a code-capable file runs its code. So the check keeps the March file at 88 but the 9 calls are still tried. A held-out check catches a changed model; it does not make a code-capable file safe to open.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The app is pinned to a numbers-only file, the firewall allows the hub alone, and every new file must score 85 of 100. In February the volunteers taught the model further on a public collection of 5,000 sentence pairs in our two languages they found on the hub, to fit village words better. The new file scored 90 of 100 and went live. Last week a clinic letter came out with the opening hours changed, and so did two others since.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did a file that scored 90 still change the clinic letters, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The examples it learned from were tampered with, so the model learned the tampering
The held-out set had no sentences like the ones that broke, so add targeted tests
Treat data like the model: know where it came from, check it, and pin it

coldCase.model: The pin and format protected the file, but the model was taught on a public collection nobody checked, and if those examples were tampered with, the model learned the tampering: data poisoning, OWASP LLM04:2025. Look through the training data for pairs whose times or hours differ between the two sides. The held-out set had no sentences like the ones that broke, so a score of 90 could not see it; add targeted tests for the sentences that matter most, opening hours, dates, doses and clinic instructions, and require them all to pass. Treat data like the model: provenance you can state, who made it and where it came from, a checksum for the exact version you used, and a person checking a sample before training. Roll back to the pinned file that passed before February.

OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning, read 15 October 2026: Data poisoning occurs when pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated to introduce vulnerabilities; Vet data vendors rigorously, and validate model outputs against trusted sources to detect signs of poisoning; Use data version control (DVC) to track changes in datasets and detect manipulation

Python documentation, pickle: Python object serialization, Warning, read 15 October 2026: The pickle module is not secure. Only unpickle data you trust; Never unpickle data that could have come from an untrusted source, or that could have been tampered with
Hugging Face, Safetensors documentation, read 15 October 2026: Safetensors is a new simple format for storing tensors safely (as opposed to pickle) and that is still fast (zero-copy)
